# Regime extrapolation: angle of attack and stall {#sec-regime-extrapolation}

**Trained on one flow regime, neither ISLA nor GeoTransolver
predicts the other.** Crossing from low to high angle of attack, or from
attached to separated flow, multiplies surface-pressure error by roughly
ten for both architectures, to a level worse than ISLA reaches from only 35
training cases inside the regime. The data-efficiency advantage of
@sec-data-efficiency does not carry across a regime boundary, and no
architectural choice tested here substitutes for training data that covers
the regime. This chapter defines the two extrapolation splits, states the
one-shot sealed-test protocol, presents the result and its three readings,
and closes the one mechanism question the result raises: GeoTransolver's
smaller degradation ratio is not carried by its raw-coordinate inputs.

## Two splits, one sealed evaluation

The question is whether a surrogate trained on attached-flow cases can
predict the pressure field of the same wing family once the flow separates.
HiLiftAeroML (@sec-problem, @sec-splits) makes this measurable because its
1,800 cases are 180 high-lift wing geometries each simulated at ten angles
of attack from 4° to 22°, and the dataset ships two curated partitions along
that axis.

The **aoa split** partitions by angle of attack. Its training set is 788
cases at angles of attack of 12° or less, its validation set is 112 further
cases from the same low-angle population, and its sealed test set is all 900
cases at 14° or more. The **stall split** partitions by flow state rather
than by angle: 942 training cases and 135 validation cases labelled
pre-stall by the dataset, and a sealed test set of 723 post-stall cases.
The two splits ask related but distinct questions. The aoa split moves the
inflow angle past the training range; the stall split holds the boundary at
the physical transition, so a post-stall case at a modest angle on a
stall-prone geometry lands in the test set while a higher-angle attached
case on a benign geometry stays in training.

In each split the validation set is *in-regime*: it is drawn from the
training population, so the validation error measures how well the model
has learned the regime it was shown, and the test error measures how far it
carries beyond it. The ratio of the two isolates the extrapolation cost
from the in-regime fit.

Training follows the frozen protocol of @sec-protocol for both
architectures: 10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bf16, no
augmentation, learning rate 1e-3 for both ISLA and GeoTransolver (each one's
best on the full split, chosen by validation before these runs), seeds 42
and 43. ISLA runs in its default configuration (constant reference length,
similarity gauge off) at 8.9M parameters and GeoTransolver at 9.0M, both at
10,000 tokens per case (@sec-mt2, @sec-baselines); peak training memory at
this token count is 1.5 GB for ISLA against 4.6 GB for GeoTransolver. The
comparison is matched on parameters, tokens and epochs.

The sealed test was run under a protocol declared before any test case was
read: the eight trained checkpoints (two splits × two architectures × two
seeds) were each evaluated exactly once on their own split's test list,
taken verbatim from the dataset manifest, with the frozen inference
configuration (10,000 sampled points, the validation-identical sampling
seed). No reruns, no configuration changes after the numbers were seen, and
no data-efficiency run touched the test lists. Every prediction was finite.

## The result: an order of magnitude on both axes {#sec-review-regime-extrapolation}

The quantity throughout is the relative L2 error of surface pressure as
defined in @sec-metrics, computed per case over its 10,000 sampled points
and averaged arithmetically over the cases of a split. The degradation
ratio is

$$
d = \frac{\text{sealed-test pressure rel-L2 (other regime)}}
         {\text{validation pressure rel-L2 (training regime)}},
$$

computed per seed and reported as the seed mean, so d = 10 means the model
is ten times less accurate on the other side of the boundary than on held-out
cases from its own side.

| split | architecture | validation (in-regime) | sealed test (OOD) | d = test / val |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aoa | GeoTransolver | 0.0301 | 0.315 | 10.5 |
| aoa | ISLA | 0.0207 | 0.244 | 11.8 |
| stall | GeoTransolver | 0.0296 | 0.276 | 9.3 |
| stall | ISLA | 0.0207 | 0.260 | 12.5 |

: Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML: seed-mean pressure rel-L2 on the
in-regime validation set and on the sealed test set of the other regime,
and their ratio d. Two seeds per cell; the per-seed values are the
individual lines of @fig-hilift-ood. Validation from
`results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json`; test and d from
`results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json`, whose `protocol` and
`inference_config` entries record the sealed-test declaration alongside
the numbers. {#tbl-hilift-ood}

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-ood
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML under the one-shot sealed test.
#|   Left: the aoa split (788 training cases at 12° or less; 112 in-regime
#|   validation cases; 900 sealed test cases at 14° or more). Right: the
#|   stall split (942 pre-stall training cases; 135 in-regime validation
#|   cases; 723 sealed post-stall test cases). Each line is one seed, joining
#|   its in-regime validation pressure error to its sealed-test pressure
#|   error; filled markers are seed 42, open markers seed 43; red circles are
#|   GeoTransolver, blue squares ISLA. Each end is annotated with
#|   the seed-mean error and each line pair with the seed-mean d = test / val.
#|   What it does not show:
#|   per-case pairing or statistics (each point is a split mean over two
#|   seeds); anything about data efficiency (@fig-hilift-data-efficiency);
#|   velocity or wall-shear error. Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface points
#|   per case, 500 epochs, bf16, no augmentation, learning rate 1e-3 for both
#|   architectures, ISLA in its default constant-gauge configuration. Data:
#|   results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json (validation) and
#|   results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json (test, d).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
sealed = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json"))
runs = sealed["runs"]
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o"), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s")}
seeds = (42, 43)
# In-regime validation sizes come from the dataset's curated split manifests
# (112 low-angle cases for aoa, 135 pre-stall cases for stall); the sealed
# test sizes are read from the artifact.
n_val = {"aoa": 112, "stall": 135}
panels = [("aoa", "Angle-of-attack extrapolation\n(train at 12° or less, test at 14° or more)"),
          ("stall", "Stall extrapolation\n(train pre-stall, test post-stall)")]
X_VAL, X_TEST = 0.0, 1.0  # the only two x positions used; no per-series offsets

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 4.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (axis, title) in zip(axs, panels):
    n_test = {runs[f"lad_hl_{a}_{axis}_seed{s}"]["n_test"] for a in style for s in seeds}
    assert len(n_test) == 1
    n_test = n_test.pop()
    for arch, (c, name, mk) in style.items():
        vals, tests, ds = [], [], []
        for s in seeds:
            key = f"lad_hl_{arch}_{axis}_seed{s}"
            v, t, d = lad[key]["pressure_l2"], runs[key]["pressure_l2"], runs[key]["d_axis"]
            assert abs(v - runs[key]["val_pressure_l2"]) < 1e-6  # the sealed-test file carries the same val number
            vals.append(v); tests.append(t); ds.append(d)
            face = c if s == 42 else "white"  # filled = seed 42, open = seed 43
            ax.plot([X_VAL, X_TEST], [v, t], color=c, lw=1.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
            ax.plot([X_VAL, X_TEST], [v, t], ls="none", marker=mk, ms=7, mfc=face, mec=c, mew=1.6, zorder=4)
        vmean, tmean, dmean = (statistics.mean(x) for x in (vals, tests, ds))
        # Direct labels: seed-mean validation error left of the validation end,
        # seed-mean test error and d right of the test end. GeoTransolver sits
        # above ISLA at both ends, so its labels go above and ISLA's below.
        up = arch == "gt"
        ax.text(X_VAL - 0.06, vmean, f"{vmean:.3f}", color=c, fontsize=8.8, ha="right",
                va="bottom" if up else "top")
        ax.text(X_TEST + 0.10, tmean * (1.30 if up else 0.78),
                f"{name}\n{tmean:.3f} on test,  d = {dmean:.1f}", color=c, fontsize=9.0,
                fontweight="bold", ha="left", va="center", linespacing=1.3)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks([X_VAL, X_TEST])
    ax.set_xticklabels([f"in-regime validation\n({n_val[axis]} cases)", f"sealed OOD test\n({n_test} cases)"])
    ax.set_xlim(-0.55, 2.35)
    ax.set_title(title, color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10.5, pad=8)
    ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor"); ax.grid(False, axis="x")
axs[0].set_yticks([0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5])
axs[0].set_yticklabels(["0.02", "0.03", "0.05", "0.10", "0.20", "0.30", "0.50"])
axs[0].set_ylim(0.015, 0.6)
axs[0].set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]  (log)", color=INK2)
fig.suptitle("Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML: one-shot sealed test, one line per seed",
             x=0.02, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=11)
fig.text(0.02, 0.02,
         "Filled markers: seed 42. Open markers: seed 43. Left end of each line: pressure error on held-out cases from the\n"
         "training regime. Right end: error on the sealed test split of the other regime, evaluated exactly once.\n"
         "d = test / validation, seed mean.",
         fontsize=7.6, color=MUTED, va="bottom", linespacing=1.35)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.09, right=0.99, bottom=0.27, top=0.80, wspace=0.08)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="How to read this figure"}
It says: *from either side of a regime boundary, both architectures lose
about a factor of ten.* The lower blue endpoints show that ISLA is still the
more accurate model on the far side of the boundary; the shallower red
slope shows that GeoTransolver loses a smaller multiple of a worse starting
point. It does not show data efficiency, per-case statistics, or any field
other than pressure, and it is a two-seed, one-shot measurement.
:::

Three readings follow, in order of importance.

**Neither architecture generalizes across a flow-regime boundary.** Both
lose a factor of about ten, from 0.021–0.030 in regime to 0.24–0.33 on the
sealed test. Those test errors are worse than ISLA reaches from 35 in-regime
training cases on the shared validation set of the data-efficiency ladder
(0.138; @sec-data-efficiency). A model that has seen 788 or 942 cases of
the wrong regime is therefore less useful than one that has seen 35 cases
spanning both regimes. Coverage of the regime, not architecture, governs this
axis. The other fields degrade in the same way: sealed-test velocity
rel-L2 is 0.19–0.26 and wall-shear rel-L2 0.32–0.39 for all eight
checkpoints, against 0.04–0.06 and 0.07–0.10 in regime.

**ISLA keeps the lower absolute error on both axes.** Its seed-mean
sealed-test pressure error is 0.244 against GeoTransolver's 0.315 on the
aoa split and 0.260 against 0.276 on the stall split. Written as
GeoTransolver error ÷ ISLA error, so that a value above 1 favours ISLA, the
advantage is 1.43–1.45 on the in-regime validation sets (between the
210-case and 1,260-case rungs of the data-efficiency ladder, as expected for
training sets of 788–942 cases) and shrinks to 1.29 on the aoa test set and
1.06 on the stall test set; it does not invert.

**GeoTransolver has the smaller degradation ratio, and it has it because
its in-regime floor is higher.** Its d is 10.5 and 9.3 against ISLA's 11.8
and 12.5. The two architectures converge to similar sealed-test error
(GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA of 1.29 on aoa and 1.06 on stall) from different
starting points (0.030 against 0.021), and a ratio criterion rewards the
worse starting point: a model that fits its own regime less well has less to
lose. The d values themselves are separated by more than their seed spread
on the stall split (d_GT / d_MT2 is 0.74 with disjoint seed intervals,
against 0.89 on aoa), so the smaller ratio is a real feature of
GeoTransolver's numbers; the next section tests whether it is carried by
GeoTransolver's raw-coordinate inputs and finds that it is not. In absolute
terms, the number that governs deployment, ISLA is ahead.

The readings carry their own limits. The measurement is two seeds and one
evaluation per checkpoint, with no per-case pairing. The two-seed intervals
are disjoint in every cell of the table, but two seeds cannot bound the
spread, so the ten-fold degradation and the 1.29 aoa ratio are robust while
the 1.06 stall ratio between architectures should be read as suggestive. Both splits
are drawn from one high-lift wing family; the conclusion is about crossing
a regime boundary within that family, not about cross-family transfer,
which is treated in @sec-full-data.

## The smaller ratio is not carried by raw coordinates {#sec-ood-mechanism}

**Giving ISLA a raw-coordinate input channel does not give it
GeoTransolver's smaller degradation ratio; the variant's d is 12.7 and 13.3
against ISLA's 12.5 and GeoTransolver's 9.3, and its sealed-test error is
unchanged (0.264 against 0.260).** GeoTransolver's smaller ratio is therefore the arithmetic
of a higher in-regime floor, not a transfer mechanism that its inputs carry.

The hypothesis under test was that GeoTransolver's inputs explain its
ratio. GeoTransolver consumes raw centered coordinates and normals per
point; ISLA consumes only SE(3)-invariant seeds relative to a gauge
(@sec-mt2). Pointwise raw-coordinate features might let a model carry a
learned map from position on the wing to pressure across the boundary, at
the cost of the in-regime accuracy that invariant seeds buy. The controlled
test adds the raw coordinates to ISLA rather than removing them from
GeoTransolver, because an added channel changes less than a removed encoder
input.

The **raw-coordinate variant** is ISLA with a side channel that appends the
gauge-normalized raw coordinates and normal components to its seed
invariants, deliberately breaking rotation equivariance (a contract test
asserts that equivariance is broken), run with the similarity gauge on
rather than the constant reference length of the reference ISLA. It was
trained on the stall split at two seeds under the otherwise frozen
protocol, with one permitted sealed-test evaluation of the two new
checkpoints only; no previously evaluated checkpoint was re-evaluated. The
stall split is the test bed because it is the axis on which the two
architectures' ratios are separated above seed spread. The readouts are the
in-regime validation pressure error, the sealed-test pressure error, and d.

The bars were declared in readout units before the variant was trained. Raw
features carry the transfer if the variant's d moves at least halfway from
ISLA's 12.5 toward GeoTransolver's 9.3, that is **d ≤ 11.0, and** its
sealed-test pressure error falls below 0.245. They do not if **d ≥ 12.0 or**
the sealed-test error is 0.255 or more. Between those bands the result is
inconclusive. Because the trigger for the test was a ratio driven by
GeoTransolver's higher denominator, the absolute sealed-test error weighs
at least as heavily as d in the reading.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

res = Path("..") / "results"
b1 = json.load(open(res / "b1_raw_coordinate_discriminator_2026-09-07.json"))
lad = json.load(open(res / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
sealed = json.load(open(res / "hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json"))["runs"]

def ref(arch):
    keys = [f"lad_hl_{arch}_stall_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)]
    v = statistics.mean(lad[k]["pressure_l2"] for k in keys)
    t = statistics.mean(sealed[k]["pressure_l2"] for k in keys)
    d = statistics.mean(sealed[k]["d_axis"] for k in keys)
    return v, t, d

lines = ["| configuration (stall split) | in-regime validation | sealed post-stall test | d = test / val |",
         "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
n_test = []
for s in (42, 43):
    r = b1[f"b1_hl_mt2_stall_rawcoord_seed{s}"]
    n_test.append(r["stall_test"]["n"])
    lines.append(f"| ISLA + raw-coordinate channel, seed {s} | {r['val']['pressure_l2']:.4f} "
                 f"| {r['stall_test']['pressure_l2']:.3f} | {r['d_axis']:.1f} |")
for arch, name in (("mt2", "ISLA reference (constant gauge), seed mean"), ("gt", "GeoTransolver, seed mean")):
    v, t, d = ref(arch)
    lines.append(f"| {name} | {v:.4f} | {t:.3f} | {d:.1f} |")
caption = (": Raw-coordinate variant of ISLA on the stall split against the reference rows of "
           "@tbl-hilift-ood: pressure rel-L2 on the 135 in-regime validation cases, on the sealed "
           "post-stall test, and their ratio d. Preregistered bars: raw coordinates carry the ratio "
           "if d ≤ 11.0 and test error < 0.245; they do not if d ≥ 12.0 or test error ≥ 0.255. "
           f"The variant's artifact records {n_test[0]} (seed 42) and {n_test[1]} (seed 43) evaluated "
           "test cases; the reference rows are means over the full 723-case test list. Data: "
           "results/b1_raw_coordinate_discriminator_2026-09-07.json (variant); "
           "results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json and "
           "results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json (reference rows). {#tbl-hilift-rawcoord}")
display(Markdown("\n".join(lines) + "\n\n" + caption))
```

Both falsifier conditions fire on both seeds: d is 12.7 and 13.3 (≥ 12.0)
and the sealed-test pressure error is 0.262 and 0.267 (≥ 0.255). The
channel leaves in-regime accuracy where the reference ISLA has it
(0.0206/0.0201 against 0.0204/0.0210) and leaves the sealed-test error
where it was (0.264 seed mean against 0.260), so the slightly larger d is
the arithmetic of a marginally lower denominator, not of any change in
out-of-regime accuracy. Raw-coordinate inputs do not buy ISLA any of
GeoTransolver's ratio. Whether the similarity gauge, on in this variant and
off in the reference, contributes to the small test-error shift is not
separated by this design; the in-regime figures say it did not move the
floor.

The reading of the previous section stands without a mechanism to add.
GeoTransolver reaches the same sealed-test error as ISLA to within 1.06x
from an in-regime floor 1.43x higher, and that is the whole of its smaller
ratio. On the absolute readout there is no transfer advantage to explain,
so no GeoTransolver ablation removing its raw coordinates is warranted. The
outcome bears on mechanism, not on the practical conclusion: every variant
tested sits at a sealed-test error near 0.26–0.28, ten or more times its
in-regime error.

## Extrapolating across boundary-condition content is a different question

Extrapolation across the *content* of the boundary data is a different
question from extrapolation across a flow regime. On linear problems with
exact labels, a decoder that evaluates the governing operator's Green's
function exactly generalizes across boundary-condition content where
soft-slice architectures do not; that route is closed for separated 3D
flow, where no exact operator is available (@sec-interior-negatives). No
architecture in this book has a mechanism for crossing a regime boundary,
and none was expected to.

## What this means in practice

**A regime boundary must be covered by training data; the surrogate's
in-regime accuracy does not predict its accuracy on the other side.** Two
consequences follow for anyone deploying either architecture on high-lift
aerodynamics.

First, training-set design matters more than architecture on this axis. A
few dozen post-stall cases are worth more than hundreds of additional
attached-flow cases if post-stall predictions are needed: the 35-case
in-regime error (0.138) is lower than the 788-case out-of-regime error
(0.244). The data-efficiency result of @sec-data-efficiency says how few
in-regime cases ISLA needs; this chapter says that none of them can be
replaced by cases from the wrong regime.

Second, a validation set drawn from the training regime overstates the
model's range by an order of magnitude. Any reported accuracy for these
surrogates should state the angle-of-attack and flow-state coverage of the
training data alongside the error, and deployment should include an
out-of-regime check on a small sealed set, evaluated once, as done here.
Within that coverage ISLA is the more accurate model (at 1.5 GB peak
training memory against GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB); outside it, neither is
usable, and the choice between them is not the decision that matters.
